_Backtick quoted variables_

Backtick quoted variables are parsed as literal Python code and are converted
internally to a Python valid identifier. This can lead to the following
problems.

During parsing a number of disallowed characters inside the backtick quoted
string are replaced by strings that are allowed as a Python identifier. These
characters include all operators in Python, the space character, the question
mark, the exclamation mark, the dollar sign, and the euro sign. For other
characters that fall outside the ASCII range (U+0001..U+007F) and those that
are not further specified in PEP 3131, the query parser will raise an error.
This excludes whitespace different than the space character, but also the
hashtag (as it is used for comments) and the backtick itself (backtick can
also not be escaped).

In a special case, quotes that make a pair around a backtick can confuse the
parser. For example, ` `it's`  > `that's`  ` will raise an error, as it forms
a quoted string ( ` 's  > `that'  ` ) with a backtick inside.

See also the Python documentation about lexical analysis ( [
https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html
](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html) ) in combination
with the source code in ` pandas.core.computation.parsing  ` .

Examples

    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame({'A': range(1, 6),
    ...                    'B': range(10, 0, -2),
    ...                    'C C': range(10, 5, -1)})
    >>> df
       A   B  C C
    0  1  10   10
    1  2   8    9
    2  3   6    8
    3  4   4    7
    4  5   2    6
    >>> df.query('A > B')
       A  B  C C
    4  5  2    6
    

The previous expression is equivalent to

    
    
    >>> df[df.A > df.B]
       A  B  C C
    4  5  2    6
    

For columns with spaces in their name, you can use backtick quoting.

    
    
    >>> df.query('B == `C C`')
       A   B  C C
    0  1  10   10
    

The previous expression is equivalent to

    
    
    >>> df[df.B == df['C C']]
       A   B  C C
    0  1  10   10

# CSSStyleDeclaration string properties all have `| null` type declaration. See original GitHub issue `lib.dom.d.ts` has recently suffixed all of the properties of `CSSStyleDeclaration` with `| null`: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/blob/master/lib/lib.dom.d.ts#L1382 https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/commit/6814c1d883791a1ad976f3146315de30e00dc0b9 For those of us using `--strictNullChecks`, this is forcing a null assertion (!) every time a property is used, even though according to the spec `null` will never be returned, only an empty string: https://drafts.csswg.org/cssom/#dom-cssstyledeclaration-getpropertyvalue > The camel-cased attribute attribute, on getting, must return the result of invoking getPropertyValue() with the argument being the result of running the IDL attribute to CSS property algorithm for camel-cased attribute. The spec does seem to allow `null` as an argument for `setPropertyValue`, so technically this a case where allowing a different type for a getter and setter (#2521) would be required to accurately model a builtin. ](https://github.com/pandas-
dev/pandas/blob/v2.2.2/pandas/core/indexes/datetimelike.py#L112-L123) #

    

Return the frequency object as a string if itâs set, otherwise None.

Examples

For DatetimeIndex:

    
    
    >>> idx = pd.DatetimeIndex(["1/1/2020 10:00:00+00:00"], freq="D")
    >>> idx.freqstr
    'D'
    

The frequency can be inferred if there are more than 2 points:

    
    
    >>> idx = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2018-01-01", "2018-01-03", "2018-01-05"],
    ...                        freq="infer")
    >>> idx.freqstr
    '2D'
    

For PeriodIndex:

    
    
    >>> idx = pd.PeriodIndex(["2023-1", "2023-2", "2023-3"], freq="M")
    >>> idx.freqstr
    'M'

#  pandas.DataFrame.mask  #

DataFrame.  mask  (  _ cond  _ , _ other  =  _NoDefault.no_default  _ , _ *  _
, _ inplace  =  False  _ , _ axis  =  None  _ , _ level  =  None  _ )  [
[source]  ](https://github.com/pandas-
dev/pandas/blob/v2.2.2/pandas/core/generic.py#L11022-L11079) #

    

Replace values where the condition is True.

Parameters  :

    

**cond** bool Series/DataFrame, array-like, or callable

    

Where  cond  is False, keep the original value. Where True, replace with
corresponding value from  other  . If  cond  is callable, it is computed on
the Series/DataFrame and should return boolean Series/DataFrame or array. The
callable must not change input Series/DataFrame (though pandas doesnât check
it).

**other** scalar, Series/DataFrame, or callable

    

Entries where  cond  is True are replaced with corresponding value from  other
. If other is callable, it is computed on the Series/DataFrame and should
return scalar or Series/DataFrame. The callable must not change input
Series/DataFrame (though pandas doesnât check it). If not specified, entries
will be filled with the corresponding NULL value ( ` np.nan  ` for numpy
dtypes, ` pd.NA  ` for extension dtypes).

**inplace** bool, default False

    

Whether to perform the operation in place on the data.

**axis** int, default None

    

Alignment axis if needed. For  Series  this parameter is unused and defaults
to 0.

**level** int, default None

    

Alignment level if needed.

Returns  :

    

Same type as caller or None if ` inplace=True  ` .

    

See also

[ ` DataFrame.where()  ` ](pandas.DataFrame.where.html#pandas.DataFrame.where
"pandas.DataFrame.where")

    

Return an object of same shape as self.

Notes

The mask method is an application of the if-then idiom. For each element in
the calling DataFrame, if ` cond  ` is ` False  ` the element is used;
otherwise the corresponding element from the DataFrame ` other  ` is used. If
the axis of ` other  ` does not align with axis of ` cond  ` Series/DataFrame,
the misaligned index positions will be filled with True.

The signature for [ ` DataFrame.where()  `
](pandas.DataFrame.where.html#pandas.DataFrame.where "pandas.DataFrame.where")
differs from [ ` numpy.where()  `
](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.where.html#numpy.where
"\(in NumPy v1.26\)") . Roughly ` df1.where(m,  df2)  ` is equivalent to `
np.where(m,  df1,  df2)  ` .

For further details and examples see the ` mask  ` documentation in [ indexing
](../../user_guide/indexing.html#indexing-where-mask) .

The dtype of the object takes precedence. The fill value is casted to the
objectâs dtype, if this can be done losslessly.

Examples

    
    
    >>> s = pd.Series(range(5))
    >>> s.where(s > 0)
    0    NaN
    1    1.0
    2    2.0
    3    3.0
    4    4.0
    dtype: float64
    >>> s.mask(s > 0)
    0    0.0
    1    NaN
    2    NaN
    3    NaN
    4    NaN
    dtype: float64
    
    
    
    >>> s = pd.Series(range(5))
    >>> t = pd.Series([True, False])
    >>> s.where(t, 99)
    0     0
    1    99
    2    99
    3    99
    4    99
    dtype: int64
    >>> s.mask(t, 99)
    0    99
    1     1
    2    99
    3    99
    4    99
    dtype: int64
    
    
    
    >>> s.where(s > 1, 10)
    0    10
    1    10
    2    2
    3    3
    4    4
    dtype: int64
    >>> s.mask(s > 1, 10)
    0     0
    1     1
    2    10
    3    10
    4    10
    dtype: int64
    
    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(10).reshape(-1, 2), columns=['A', 'B'])
    >>> df
       A  B
    0  0  1
    1  2  3
    2

# Optimizing JavaScript Build Performance in Large-Scale React Applications with Webpack

In modern front-end development, build performance has become a critical factor influencing developer productivity and deployment speed. As React applications grow in size and complexity, the time it takes to bundle, transpile, and optimize JavaScript can balloon, slowing iteration and increasing infrastructure costs. Webpack, as a sophisticated module bundler, offers an extensive set of configuration options and caching mechanisms that can be leveraged to significantly improve build times without sacrificing output quality.

## Understanding Build Bottlenecks

Large-scale React applications often suffer from slow builds due to several factors:  
- **High module count**: Hundreds or thousands of JavaScript and CSS modules must be parsed and transformed.  
- **Complex transpilation**: Babel transformations, JSX compilation, and polyfilling for multiple browser targets add processing overhead.  
- **Asset optimization**: Minification, tree-shaking, and code splitting require additional passes over the code.  

Identifying which step consumes the most time is crucial. Webpack’s built-in profiling tools (`--profile --json`) and plugins such as `webpack-bundle-analyzer` can help pinpoint bottlenecks.

## Leveraging Persistent Caching

Webpack’s `cache` configuration allows developers to enable persistent caching between builds. By setting:

```js
module.exports = {
  cache: {
    type: 'filesystem',
    buildDependencies: {
      config: [__filename],
    },
  },
};
```

Webpack stores processed modules and other build artifacts on disk. Subsequent builds can reuse these cached results, drastically reducing compilation time, especially in incremental builds during development. This approach is particularly effective for large projects where unchanged modules constitute the majority of the codebase during iterative changes.

## Parallelization and Thread Loaders

JavaScript builds often benefit from parallel processing. Tools like `thread-loader` can offload expensive transformations to worker threads, allowing Babel or TypeScript compilation to run concurrently across multiple CPU cores. This can be configured for rules that match large sets of files, for example:

```js
{
  test: /\.js$/,
  use: [
    'thread-loader',
    'babel-loader'
  ]
}
```

While parallelization introduces some overhead in spawning threads, the benefits on large codebases generally outweigh the costs.

## Optimizing Babel and Loader Configurations

Babel’s preset configurations can be tuned to avoid unnecessary transformations. For example, limiting polyfills to the specific browsers you target via `@babel/preset-env` with `targets` reduces processing time and output size. Similarly, excluding `node_modules` from heavy loaders prevents redundant work on already optimized third-party code.

Webpack’s `exclude` and `include` options in loader rules should be carefully scoped to ensure only relevant files are processed.

## Code Splitting and Dynamic Imports

While code splitting primarily optimizes runtime performance and bundle size, it can also influence build times by reducing the amount of code processed in a single chunk. By strategically applying dynamic imports, developers can isolate rarely used modules into separate bundles, lessening the work Webpack must perform on the main application bundle.

## Minimizer and Plugin Tuning

In production builds, minification is one of the most time-consuming steps. Switching to faster minimizers such as `terser-webpack-plugin` with appropriate parallelization settings can yield noticeable improvements. Configuring plugins to run only when necessary—such as image optimization plugins being enabled only in production—reduces overhead during development builds.

## Incremental and Differential Builds

For very large projects, consider breaking the application into multiple smaller builds, each with its own Webpack configuration. This modular approach allows for selective rebuilding of only the affected parts of the application. Additionally, differential builds targeting modern browsers separately from legacy ones can reduce the amount of transpilation required for most users.

## Conclusion

Optimizing JavaScript build performance in large-scale React applications requires a multi-pronged approach: identifying bottlenecks, leveraging persistent caching, parallelizing transformations, and tuning loaders and plugins. By thoughtfully configuring Webpack’s advanced features, teams can achieve faster build times, enabling more rapid iteration and smoother deployment pipelines. Over time, these optimizations not only improve developer experience but also contribute to more efficient CI/CD workflows and reduced infrastructure costs.

# Optimizing Concurrent PostgreSQL Queries with Python’s psycopg2 and Multithreading

When working with large datasets in PostgreSQL, query execution time can quickly become a bottleneck in data-intensive applications. For workloads requiring multiple independent queries—such as batch analytics, reporting pipelines, or data ingestion validation—leveraging Python’s multithreading capabilities in conjunction with the psycopg2 library can yield significant performance gains. However, to achieve optimal throughput, developers must consider both Python’s concurrency model and PostgreSQL’s configuration for parallel workloads.

## Understanding the Concurrency Landscape

Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is often cited as a limitation for CPU-bound multithreaded workloads, but database queries are typically I/O-bound. This means that threads spend much of their time waiting for network responses and database processing, allowing other threads to run in the meantime. The psycopg2 library, being a mature PostgreSQL adapter, is well-suited for managing multiple concurrent connections, each executing queries independently.

In a typical scenario, multiple threads can be spawned to execute queries in parallel, each with its own database connection. This approach allows PostgreSQL to process requests concurrently, provided the server configuration supports sufficient worker processes and connection pooling.

## Structuring Multithreaded Query Execution

The foundational step is to ensure that each thread uses a separate psycopg2 connection object. Reusing a single connection across threads can lead to contention and unexpected behavior. A simple threading pattern might look like this:

```python
import threading
import psycopg2

def run_query(query, conn_params):
    with psycopg2.connect(**conn_params) as conn:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(query)
            results = cur.fetchall()
            # Process results here

queries = [
    "SELECT * FROM large_table WHERE category = 'A';",
    "SELECT * FROM large_table WHERE category = 'B';",
    # ... more queries
]

conn_params = {
    'dbname': 'mydb',
    'user': 'dbuser',
    'password': 'secret',
    'host': 'localhost',
    'port': 5432
}

threads = []
for q in queries:
    t = threading.Thread(target=run_query, args=(q, conn_params))
    threads.append(t)
    t.start()

for t in threads:
    t.join()
```

This pattern ensures each thread operates independently, enabling PostgreSQL to handle multiple queries in parallel.

## Database-Side Performance Tuning

Even with correctly implemented multithreading in Python, PostgreSQL’s own configuration plays a pivotal role in throughput. Key parameters to review include:

- **`max_connections`**: Must be high enough to accommodate all concurrent threads without exhausting resources.
- **`work_mem`**: Increasing this allows complex queries to run more efficiently without spilling to disk.
- **`effective_cache_size`**: Helps the query planner make better decisions about index usage.
- **Parallel query settings**: Parameters like `max_parallel_workers` and `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` can improve performance for single large queries, but their impact on many small concurrent queries should be tested.

Connection pooling solutions, such as **pgBouncer** or **Pgpool-II**, can also reduce the overhead of establishing new connections in each thread, especially for short-lived queries.

## Balancing Thread Count and Server Load

While it may be tempting to spawn dozens of threads to maximize concurrency, there is a point of diminishing returns. Excessive concurrent queries can saturate network bandwidth, overload CPU resources on the database server, or cause lock contention on frequently accessed tables. Performance testing should be conducted to identify the optimal number of threads for the workload and hardware configuration.

A common approach is to start with a modest thread count—such as the number of CPU cores available on the database server—and gradually increase it while monitoring query latency, throughput, and system metrics. Tools like `pg_stat_activity` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` can provide insights into query execution behavior under load.

## Monitoring and Profiling

To sustain high performance, continuous monitoring is essential. Integrating query execution timing in the Python application, alongside PostgreSQL’s native logging, allows developers to pinpoint bottlenecks. Profiling tools such as `cProfile` in Python can identify if delays are occurring in query execution or in client-side processing.

On the database side, enabling `log_min_duration_statement` can help identify queries that consistently exceed expected execution times. Combined with indexing strategies and query plan optimization, these insights ensure that multithreaded execution remains efficient over time.

## Conclusion

Optimizing concurrent database queries with Python’s psycopg2 library is not simply a matter of adding threads—it requires careful alignment between client-side concurrency patterns and server-side configuration. By isolating connections per thread, tuning PostgreSQL parameters for parallel workloads, and balancing thread counts against system capacity, developers can unlock substantial performance improvements when handling large datasets. Ongoing monitoring and iterative tuning complete the optimization cycle, ensuring that both Python and PostgreSQL work together to deliver high-throughput, low-latency query execution.

## Drag effects When dragging, there are several operations that may be performed. The `copy` operation is used to indicate that the data being dragged will be copied from its present location to the drop location. The `move` operation is used to indicate that the data being dragged will be moved, and the `link` operation is used to indicate that some form of relationship or connection will be created between the source and drop locations. You can specify which of the three operations are allowed for a drag source by setting the `effectAllowed` property within a `dragstart` event listener. In this example, only a **copy** is allowed. You can combine the values in various ways: `none` no operation is permitted `copy` `copy` only `move` `move` only `link` `link` only `copyMove` `copy` or `move` only `copyLink` `copy` or `link` only `linkMove` `link` or `move` only `all` `copy`, `move`, or `link` `uninitialized` the default value when the effect has not been set, equivalent to `all` Note that these values must be used exactly as listed above. For example, setting the `effectAllowed` property to `copyMove` allows a copy or move operation but prevents the user from performing a link operation. If you don't change the `effectAllowed` property, then any operation is allowed, just like with the `all` value. So you don't need to adjust this property unless you want to exclude specific types. During a drag operation, a listener for the `dragenter` or `dragover` events can check the `effectAllowed` property to see which operations are permitted. A related property, `dropEffect`, should be set within one of these events to specify which single operation should be performed. Valid values for `dropEffect` are `none`, `copy`, `move`, or `link`. The combination values are not used for this property. With the `dragenter` and `dragover` event, the `dropEffect` property is initialized to the effect that the user is requesting. The user can modify the desired effect by pressing modifier keys. Although the exact keys used vary by platform, typically the `Shift` and `Control` keys would be used to switch between copying, moving, and linking. The mouse pointer will change to indicate which operation is desired. For instance, for a `copy`, the cursor might appear with a plus sign next to it. You can modify the `dropEffect` property during the `dragenter` or `dragover` events, if for example, a particular drop target only supports certain operations. You can modify the `dropEffect` property to override the user effect, and enforce a specific drop operation to occur. Note that this effect must be one listed within the `effectAllowed` property. Otherwise, it will be set to an alternate value that is allowed. In this example, copy is the effect that is performed. You can use the value `none` to indicate that no drop is allowed at this location, although it is preferred not to cancel the event in this case. Within the `drop` and `dragend` events, you can check the `dropEffect` property to determine which effect was ultimately chosen. If the chosen effect were `move`, then the original data should be removed from the source of the drag within the `dragend` event. ## Specifying drop targets A listener for the `dragenter` and `dragover` events are used to indicate valid drop targets, that is, places where dragged items may be dropped. Most areas of a web page or application are not valid places to drop data. Thus, the default handling of these events is not to allow a drop. If you want to allow a drop, you must prevent the default behavior by cancelling both the `dragenter` and `dragover` events. You can do this by calling their `preventDefault()`") methods: Calling the `preventDefault()`") method during both the `dragenter` and `dragover` event will indicate that a drop is allowed at that location. However, you will commonly wish to call the `preventDefault()`") method only in certain situations (for example, only if a link is being dragged). To do this, call a function which checks a condition and only cancels the event when the condition is met. If the condition is not met, don't cancel the event, and a drop will not occur there if the user releases the mouse button. It is most common to accept or reject a drop based on the type of drag data in the data transfer — for instance, allowing images, or links, or both. To do this, you can check the `types` property of the event's `dataTransfer` (property). The `types` property returns an array of the string types that were added when the drag began, in the order from most significant to least significant. In this example, we use the `includes` method to check if the type `text/uri-list` is present in the list of types. If it is, we will cancel the event so that a drop may be allowed. If the drag data does not contain a link, the event will not be cancelled, and a drop cannot occur at that location. You may also wish to set either the `effectAllowed`, `dropEffect` property, or both at the same time, if you wish to be more specific about the type of operation that will performed. Naturally, changing either property will have no effect if you do not cancel the event as well.

**Leading Development Teams: Strategies for Effective Management**  

Managing a team of software developers requires a blend of technical awareness, leadership skills, and emotional intelligence. While deep coding knowledge can be an asset, the most successful leaders focus on creating an environment where developers can thrive, collaborate, and deliver high-quality projects on time. This post explores three key pillars of effective software team management: leadership qualities, communication styles, and delegation techniques.  

---

### Leadership Qualities That Inspire  
In the fast-paced world of software development, a leader must balance vision with adaptability. Clear direction is essential, but so is the ability to adjust course when requirements shift or new challenges arise. Effective leaders exhibit:  

- **Empathy and Understanding**: Recognizing the pressures developers face, from tight deadlines to complex problem-solving, and providing support when needed.  
- **Transparency**: Being open about project goals, challenges, and changes builds trust and keeps the team aligned.  
- **Decisiveness**: Making timely decisions reduces bottlenecks and keeps development moving forward.  

A good leader also models resilience—showing the team how to navigate setbacks without losing momentum. This not only strengthens morale but also encourages developers to take ownership of their work.  

---

### Communication Styles for Development Teams  
Communication is the backbone of any successful development effort. Leaders must tailor their communication style to the needs of the team and the nature of the work. Three approaches stand out:  

1. **Structured Updates**: Regular stand-ups or progress meetings keep everyone informed. These should be brief and focused, ensuring developers spend most of their time building rather than reporting.  
2. **Open-Door Policy**: Creating an environment where developers feel comfortable raising issues or suggesting improvements fosters innovation and problem-solving.  
3. **Clear Documentation**: Well-maintained documentation reduces misunderstandings, especially when onboarding new team members or collaborating across departments.  

Leaders who actively listen and respond constructively help maintain a culture of trust and collaboration. It’s important to balance formal communication channels with informal check-ins, ensuring both project and personal concerns are addressed.  

---

### Delegation Techniques for Effective Delivery  
Delegation in software development is not merely assigning tasks—it’s about empowering team members to take responsibility and make decisions within their domain of expertise. Effective delegation involves:  

- **Matching Tasks to Skill Sets**: Assigning work that aligns with a developer’s strengths while also offering opportunities for growth.  
- **Defining Clear Outcomes**: Instead of micromanaging every step, focus on the desired end result and allow developers to choose the best path to achieve it.  
- **Providing Resources and Support**: Ensuring the team has the tools, information, and authority needed to complete their tasks successfully.  

Delegation also requires trust. Leaders must believe in their team’s capabilities and resist the urge to intervene unnecessarily. This not only speeds up delivery but also builds confidence and autonomy among developers.  

---

### Bringing It All Together  
A well-managed software development team thrives when leadership qualities, communication styles, and delegation techniques are in harmony. Leaders set the tone by inspiring and guiding, communication keeps the team connected and informed, and delegation empowers individuals to excel.  

By fostering a culture of respect, openness, and shared responsibility, managers can transform a group of developers into a cohesive, high-performing team. The result is not just efficient project delivery, but a workplace where creativity, innovation, and professional growth are part of the daily experience.  

Ultimately, while tools, methodologies, and frameworks play an important role in software development, it’s the human element—how leaders interact with their teams—that determines long-term success. Investing in leadership development, refining communication practices, and mastering the art of delegation are the keys to building sustainable, productive, and motivated development teams.

# Efficient JSON Handling in PostgreSQL with Django ORM

PostgreSQL’s native support for JSON and JSONB data types has opened up flexible avenues for storing semi-structured data while still benefiting from relational database guarantees. When integrated with Django’s ORM, developers can serialize complex Python objects into JSON and persist them efficiently, while retaining powerful querying capabilities. This article explores practical strategies for serializing, storing, and optimizing JSON records in PostgreSQL using Django, with a focus on indexing and query performance for large datasets.

---

## Serializing Data for Storage

Django provides built-in support for JSON fields through `django.db.models.JSONField`, available in Django 3.1 and above. This field type automatically handles serialization and deserialization between Python objects and JSON strings. For example, a Python list or dictionary can be assigned directly to the field, and Django will serialize it into JSON when saving to the database.

Under the hood, when using PostgreSQL, the JSONField maps to the `jsonb` column type. This binary JSON format is more efficient for storage and querying than plain JSON, offering advantages such as faster access to nested keys and support for advanced indexing.

For older Django versions or custom needs, developers can manually serialize Python objects using Python’s `json` module before saving them into a `TextField` or `BinaryField`. This approach requires explicit deserialization when retrieving records.

---

## Indexing JSON Data

Storing JSON records is straightforward, but querying them at scale demands thoughtful indexing. PostgreSQL supports Generalized Inverted Indexes (GIN) for `jsonb` columns, allowing rapid lookups on keys and values within JSON structures.

For example, if you frequently query for records containing a certain key or value, you can create a GIN index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX data_gin_idx ON my_table USING GIN (my_json_column);
```

This index accelerates queries using the `@>` containment operator, which checks whether one JSON document contains another. For instance:

```sql
SELECT * FROM my_table
WHERE my_json_column @> '{"status": "active"}';
```

Partial indexes can be used when only a subset of records needs to be searchable, reducing index size and improving write performance.

---

## Query Optimization Techniques

Querying large JSON datasets can become expensive if not optimized. Here are several strategies:

1. **Key-specific indexes**: Instead of indexing the entire JSON document, create expression indexes on specific keys.  
   ```sql
   CREATE INDEX idx_status ON my_table ((my_json_column->>'status'));
   ```

2. **Avoid unnecessary nesting**: Deeply nested JSON structures require more processing to traverse. Flatten structures where possible to improve query speed.

3. **Use `jsonb_path_ops`**: This GIN operator class optimizes indexing for containment queries, offering smaller index sizes and faster lookups for certain workloads.

4. **Selective retrieval**: Use Django’s `.values()` or `.only()` to fetch only the fields needed for processing, reducing data transfer overhead.

---

## Managing Large Datasets

When dealing with millions of JSON records, performance tuning becomes critical. Batch inserts using Django’s `bulk_create()` can reduce overhead when inserting large volumes of JSON data. Likewise, batch updates with `bulk_update()` minimize transaction costs.

For analytical workloads, consider materialized views that precompute common queries on JSON data. These views can be refreshed periodically to balance query speed with data freshness.

Another approach is hybrid storage: store frequently queried attributes in dedicated columns alongside the JSON field. This enables faster filtering and sorting while retaining the flexibility of JSON for less-structured data.

---

## Django ORM Integration

Django’s ORM provides filters and lookups tailored for PostgreSQL’s JSON capabilities. For example:

```python
MyModel.objects.filter(my_json_field__status='active')
```

Behind the scenes, Django translates this into a `->>` operator query against the `jsonb` column. Combined with proper indexing, these lookups can be highly performant.

For more complex queries, Django’s `KeyTransform` and `KeyTextTransform` functions allow deeper access into nested JSON structures while still leveraging ORM syntax.

---

## Conclusion

By combining Django’s JSONField with PostgreSQL’s robust JSONB support, developers can store and query semi-structured data efficiently. The key to scaling lies in careful indexing — whether through GIN indexes, key-specific indexes, or partial indexes — and optimizing queries to minimize unnecessary data traversal. For large datasets, batching operations and hybrid storage models can further enhance performance. This synergy between Django’s ORM and PostgreSQL’s JSON capabilities enables applications to handle flexible data models without sacrificing speed or maintainability.

**ambiguous** âinferâ, bool-ndarray, âNaTâ, default âraiseâ

    

Only relevant for DatetimeIndex:

  * âinferâ will attempt to infer fall dst-transition hours based on order 

  * bool-ndarray where True signifies a DST time, False designates a non-DST time (note that this flag is only applicable for ambiguous times) 

  * âNaTâ will return NaT where there are ambiguous times 

  * âraiseâ will raise an AmbiguousTimeError if there are ambiguous times. 

**nonexistent** âshift_forwardâ, âshift_backwardâ, âNaTâ,
timedelta, default âraiseâ

    

A nonexistent time does not exist in a particular timezone where clocks moved
forward due to DST.

  * âshift_forwardâ will shift the nonexistent time forward to the closest existing time 

  * âshift_backwardâ will shift the nonexistent time backward to the closest existing time 

  * âNaTâ will return NaT where there are nonexistent times 

  * timedelta objects will shift nonexistent times by the timedelta 

  * âraiseâ will raise an NonExistentTimeError if there are nonexistent times. 

Returns  :

    

DatetimeIndex, TimedeltaIndex, or Series

    

Index of the same type for a DatetimeIndex or TimedeltaIndex, or a Series with
the same index for a Series.

Raises  :

    

ValueError if the  freq  cannot be converted.

    

Notes

If the timestamps have a timezone, flooring will take place relative to the
local (âwallâ) time and re-localized to the same timezone. When flooring
near daylight savings time, use ` nonexistent  ` and ` ambiguous  ` to control
the re-localization behavior.

Examples

**DatetimeIndex**

    
    
    >>> rng = pd.date_range('1/1/2018 11:59:00', periods=3, freq='min')
    >>> rng
    DatetimeIndex(['2018-01-01 11:59:00', '2018-01-01 12:00:00',
                   '2018-01-01 12:01:00'],
                  dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='min')
    >>> rng.floor('h')
    DatetimeIndex(['2018-01-01 11:00:00', '2018-01-01 12:00:00',
                   '2018-01-01 12:00:00'],
                  dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
    

**Series**

    
    
    >>> pd.Series(rng).dt.floor("h")
    0   2018-01-01 11:00:00
    1   2018-01-01 12:00:00
    2   2018-01-01 12:00:00
    dtype: datetime64[ns]
    

When rounding near a daylight savings time transition, use ` ambiguous  ` or `
nonexistent  ` to control how the timestamp should be re-localized.

    
    
    >>> rng_tz = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2021-10-31 03:30:00"], tz="Europe/Amsterdam")
    
    
    
    >>> rng_tz.floor("2h", ambiguous=False)
    DatetimeIndex(['2021-10-31 02:00:00+01:00'],
                 dtype='datetime64[ns, Europe/Amsterdam]', freq=None)
    
    
    
    >>> rng_tz.floor("2h", ambiguous=True)
    DatetimeIndex(['2021-10-31 02:00:00+02:00'],
                  dtype='datetime64[ns, Europe/Amsterdam]', freq=None)

# Optimizing Dashboard Refresh Strategies for Industrial Environmental Monitoring

In industrial environments, the accuracy and timeliness of sensor data are critical for operational safety, compliance, and efficiency. Graphical dashboards that visualize readings—such as temperature, humidity, particulate levels, and gas concentrations—must be designed to refresh at appropriate intervals without overloading network infrastructure or introducing latency. This post explores techniques for achieving efficient refresh cycles, focusing on network communication optimizations and hardware-triggered update mechanisms.

---

## Understanding the Refresh Challenge

Environmental monitoring systems often aggregate data from distributed sensors connected via wired or wireless networks. Dashboards in control rooms or remote terminals display real-time or near-real-time readings. The refresh interval determines how frequently data is fetched and rendered, impacting:

- **Data accuracy**: Short intervals yield fresher data but can cause unnecessary network traffic.
- **System load**: Frequent updates can burden both the network and the rendering pipeline.
- **Operator usability**: Too rapid changes can make trends hard to observe, while slow refreshes risk missing critical events.

The optimal refresh strategy balances these factors, ensuring that updates occur when meaningful changes happen, rather than purely on a timed schedule.

---

## Network Communication Protocols

Choosing the right communication protocol is foundational to refresh efficiency.

### MQTT for Publish/Subscribe Efficiency
In setups with many sensors, MQTT offers a lightweight publish/subscribe model. Sensors publish updates only when readings change beyond a defined threshold. The dashboard subscribes to relevant topics, receiving data instantly without polling. This reduces redundant transmissions and network congestion.

### WebSockets for Persistent Connections
Where dashboards require continuous streaming of high-frequency data, WebSockets enable a persistent, bidirectional connection. This eliminates the overhead of repeated HTTP requests and allows immediate push updates from the server.

### HTTP with Conditional Requests
In lower-frequency scenarios, HTTP GET requests with `If-Modified-Since` headers can be used to check for data changes before downloading payloads. This is effective when the backend can efficiently determine whether data has been updated.

---

## Hardware-Triggered Updates

While timed refreshes are common, hardware-triggered updates can significantly improve responsiveness and efficiency.

### Interrupt-Driven Sensor Communication
Many industrial sensors support hardware interrupts that signal when data changes. Integrating these interrupts into the data acquisition system allows immediate notification to the dashboard without constant polling.

### Edge Processing Units
Deploying microcontrollers or industrial PCs at the edge to process raw sensor data and detect anomalies enables intelligent update triggers. These units can push summarized or event-specific data to the dashboard, reducing bandwidth usage.

### Direct Digital Inputs to Control Systems
For critical thresholds (e.g., gas leak detection), sensors can be wired directly to control system inputs that trigger both safety protocols and dashboard updates, ensuring operators see urgent changes instantly.

---

## Refresh Interval Strategies

A hybrid approach often yields the best results:

1. **Event-Driven Updates**: Use hardware interrupts or publish/subscribe protocols to push changes as they occur.
2. **Scheduled Refreshes**: Implement periodic updates (e.g., every 5 minutes) to ensure dashboards remain synchronized even if no events are triggered.
3. **Adaptive Intervals**: Adjust refresh frequency based on operational conditions. For example, during stable periods, slow down updates; during rapid environmental changes, increase frequency.

The scheduling logic can reside in the backend service, which informs the dashboard of the next expected update, or in the dashboard client itself, which adapts based on data patterns.

---

## Implementation Considerations

- **Data Batching**: Aggregate small changes into batches before transmission to reduce overhead.
- **Compression**: Use lightweight data formats (e.g., JSON with gzip) or binary protocols (e.g., Protocol Buffers) to minimize payload size.
- **Caching**: Maintain local caches to avoid unnecessary rendering when data is unchanged.
- **Failover Mechanisms**: Ensure dashboards can fall back to scheduled polling if event-driven channels fail.

---

## Conclusion

Efficiently refreshing industrial environmental monitoring dashboards requires more than simply setting a timer. By leveraging optimized network protocols like MQTT or WebSockets, incorporating hardware-triggered events, and adopting adaptive refresh strategies, operators can maintain high situational awareness without overburdening infrastructure. The key is to align refresh mechanisms with the nature of the monitored data—updating rapidly when conditions change and conserving resources when they do not. This approach ensures dashboards remain both responsive and sustainable in demanding industrial contexts.

# Organizing and Documenting CSS Style Guidelines for Large Teams  

In large-scale front‑end projects, the complexity of maintaining consistent CSS grows exponentially with the number of contributors. Without clear rules and documentation, stylesheets can quickly become cluttered, inconsistent, and difficult to maintain. This post explores strategies for organizing and documenting CSS style guidelines so that teams can work efficiently and deliver a unified visual experience.  

## Establishing Naming Conventions  

Naming conventions form the foundation of a maintainable CSS codebase. They provide a shared language for developers and ensure that class names convey meaning. Popular methodologies such as BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) or SMACSS offer structured approaches to naming that help avoid conflicts and make styles easier to read.  

For example, BEM’s pattern (`.block__element--modifier`) clearly communicates the role of a class in the UI hierarchy. By adopting a convention and documenting it in the team’s style guide, developers can quickly identify the purpose of a selector and avoid creating redundant or ambiguous styles. Guidelines should include examples, common pitfalls, and a glossary of approved naming patterns.  

## Consistent Formatting Rules  

Beyond naming, consistent formatting ensures that stylesheets remain readable and predictable. Formatting rules can cover indentation, spacing, selector ordering, and property grouping. For instance, properties might be grouped by box model, typography, and visual appearance, with each group ordered alphabetically.  

It’s important to standardize how colors, units, and shorthand properties are expressed. For example, deciding whether to use `rem` or `px` for font sizes, or whether hex codes or `rgb()` values are preferred, prevents confusion and reduces the need for later refactoring. A team can enforce these rules through linting tools like Stylelint, which automatically flags violations and encourages adherence to the agreed‑upon standards.  

## Leveraging CSS Preprocessors  

CSS preprocessors such as Sass or Less offer powerful features that help enforce coding standards. Variables, mixins, and functions can encapsulate design tokens and repetitive patterns, ensuring consistency across components. For example, defining a single `$primary-color` variable means that color changes propagate throughout the codebase without having to hunt for hard‑coded values.  

Preprocessors also allow for modular file organization. By splitting styles into partials—for typography, layout, components, and utilities—teams can keep files small, focused, and easier to navigate. Documentation should outline the directory structure and naming scheme for these partials, as well as rules for when and how to create new ones.  

## Centralized Documentation  

Even with conventions and tools in place, clear documentation is essential. A centralized style guide should include:  

- **Naming conventions** with examples and rationale.  
- **Formatting rules** covering indentation, property order, and syntax preferences.  
- **Design tokens** such as colors, font stacks, and spacing values.  
- **Component library references** with code snippets and usage guidelines.  
- **Preprocessor patterns** (variables, mixins, functions) and their intended use cases.  

This documentation can live in a shared repository, a wiki, or integrated into a design system platform. Keeping it up to date is critical—assigning ownership to specific team members ensures accountability and regular review.  

## Enforcing Guidelines Through Tooling  

Tools bridge the gap between documentation and practice. Linting, automated code formatting, and build‑time checks help catch deviations before they reach production. For example, Stylelint can be configured to enforce naming conventions, disallow inline styles, or require that properties appear in a specific order. Coupled with Prettier for formatting, these tools reduce manual review overhead and keep the codebase consistent.  

Continuous integration (CI) pipelines can run these checks automatically on pull requests, ensuring that style guidelines remain enforceable without relying solely on human oversight.  

## Conclusion  

Maintaining clear and consistent CSS style guidelines in a large team is not just about aesthetics—it’s about scalability, maintainability, and collaboration. By combining strong naming conventions, consistent formatting, preprocessors, centralized documentation, and automated enforcement, teams can build a CSS architecture that supports growth and reduces friction.  

When everyone speaks the same “CSS language,” the result is a cleaner codebase, faster onboarding, and a more cohesive user experience. The investment in defining and documenting these guidelines pays off in reduced technical debt and greater confidence in the team’s ability to deliver high‑quality interfaces.

###  Applying different functions to DataFrame columns  #

By passing a dict to ` aggregate  ` you can apply a different aggregation to
the columns of a DataFrame:

    
    
    In [115]: grouped.agg({"C": "sum", "D": lambda x: np.std(x, ddof=1)})
    Out[115]: 
                C         D
    A

##  Transformation  #

A transformation is a GroupBy operation whose result is indexed the same as
the one being grouped. Common examples include [ ` cumsum()  `
](../reference/api/pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.cumsum.html#pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.cumsum
"pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.cumsum") and [ ` diff()  `
](../reference/api/pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.diff.html#pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.diff
"pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.diff") .

    
    
    In [117]: speeds
    Out[117]: 
              class           order  max_speed
    falcon     bird   Falconiformes      389.0
    parrot     bird  Psittaciformes       24.0
    lion     mammal       Carnivora       80.2
    monkey   mammal        Primates        NaN
    leopard  mammal       Carnivora       58.0
    
    In [118]: grouped = speeds.groupby("class")["max_speed"]
    
    In [119]: grouped.cumsum()
    Out[119]: 
    falcon     389.0
    parrot     413.0
    lion        80.2
    monkey       NaN
    leopard    138.2
    Name: max_speed, dtype: float64
    
    In [120]: grouped.diff()
    Out[120]: 
    falcon       NaN
    parrot    -365.0
    lion         NaN
    monkey       NaN
    leopard      NaN
    Name: max_speed, dtype: float64
    

Unlike aggregations, the groupings that are used to split the original object
are not included in the result.

Note

Since transformations do not include the groupings that are used to split the
result, the arguments ` as_index  ` and ` sort  ` in [ ` DataFrame.groupby()
` ](../reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.groupby.html#pandas.DataFrame.groupby
"pandas.DataFrame.groupby") and [ ` Series.groupby()  `
](../reference/api/pandas.Series.groupby.html#pandas.Series.groupby
"pandas.Series.groupby") have no effect.

A common use of a transformation is to add the result back into the original
DataFrame.

    
    
    In [121]: result = speeds.copy()
    
    In [122]: result["cumsum"] = grouped.cumsum()
    
    In [123]: result["diff"] = grouped.diff()
    
    In [124]: result
    Out[124]: 
              class           order  max_speed  cumsum   diff
    falcon     bird   Falconiformes      389.0   389.0    NaN
    parrot     bird  Psittaciformes       24.0   413.0 -365.0
    lion     mammal       Carnivora       80.2    80.2    NaN
    monkey   mammal        Primates        NaN     NaN    NaN
    leopard  mammal       Carnivora       58.0   138.2    NaN

**Windows File Indexing and Metadata Storage in NTFS**  

The Windows operating system employs a combination of filesystem-level structures and dedicated indexing services to facilitate rapid search retrieval and efficient file management. While the sorting of files in graphical interfaces is a separate process, the underlying capability to locate and enumerate files quickly relies upon the way Windows stores and organizes metadata, particularly in the NTFS (New Technology File System) format.  

---

### NTFS Metadata Architecture  

NTFS is a journaling filesystem introduced with Windows NT that uses a Master File Table (MFT) as the central repository for all file and directory metadata. Each file and directory is represented by a record in the MFT, storing attributes such as file name, size, timestamps, security descriptors, and pointers to the file’s data clusters.  

File names within NTFS can be stored in multiple forms: the original name and an alternate "short name" (for compatibility with legacy applications). These names are recorded in the `$FILE_NAME` attribute of the MFT record, which also contains creation, modification, and access times. The MFT allows constant-time access to metadata, meaning the system can enumerate and retrieve file attributes without reading the actual file content.  

---

### Directory Indexing Mechanism  

Within NTFS, directories are implemented as B+ tree structures. This indexing method enables efficient searching and insertion of entries. The B+ tree for a directory organizes file name entries according to collation rules defined by the filesystem driver. These rules determine how file names are compared and ordered internally for traversal.  

When a directory contains a large number of files, the B+ tree index ensures that lookup operations scale logarithmically rather than linearly. This is crucial for responsiveness in directories with thousands of entries, as the tree enables quick location of a given name or range of names based on the indexing key.  

---

### Windows Search Indexing Service  

Beyond the filesystem-level indexing, modern Windows systems incorporate the Windows Search service, a background process that builds and maintains a separate search index database. This service scans designated locations on the disk and extracts metadata from files, such as titles, authors, and content snippets, using property handlers for different file types.  

The search index is stored in a compressed database format within the user profile, typically under `ProgramData\Microsoft\Search\Data`. It is optimized for rapid retrieval by mapping search queries to indexed terms and associated file references. The service updates the index dynamically when files are created, modified, or deleted, using NTFS change journals to detect modifications without re-scanning entire directories.  

---

### NTFS Change Journal  

The NTFS change journal, also known as the USN (Update Sequence Number) Journal, is a persistent log that records changes to files and directories. Each change—such as creation, deletion, or modification—generates a USN record. The Windows Search service relies on this journal to identify items that need re-indexing, significantly reducing the overhead of maintaining the search database.  

This journal is stored per volume and can be accessed programmatically through system APIs. It ensures that search results remain current without requiring exhaustive rescans of the filesystem.  

---

### Metadata Caching and Retrieval  

To shorten access times, Windows employs metadata caching at multiple layers. The NTFS driver maintains in-memory caches of frequently accessed directory indices and MFT segments. The Windows Search service also caches query results and term lookups to accelerate repeated searches.  

When a user performs a search through File Explorer, the system can merge results from the NTFS directory enumeration with pre-computed entries from the search index, depending on the search scope and whether indexing is enabled for the queried location.  

---

### Conclusion  

Windows achieves efficient file retrieval through a combination of NTFS’s structured metadata storage, directory B+ tree indexing, the persistent change journal, and the Windows Search service’s dedicated index database. These components work together to ensure that file attributes and content metadata are readily accessible for queries, allowing the operating system to deliver rapid results in both local and indexed searches. While the visual presentation of files in Explorer may vary depending on user settings, the underlying indexing mechanisms remain consistent, providing a robust foundation for search functionality across the platform.

#  308 Permanent Redirect

The HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) **` 308 Permanent Redirect ` **
redirect status response code indicates that the resource requested has been
definitively moved to the URL given by the [ ` Location ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Location) headers. A browser redirects to this page
and search engines update their links to the resource (in 'SEO-speak', it is
said that the 'link-juice' is sent to the new URL).

The request method and the body will not be altered, whereas [ ` 301 ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/301) may incorrectly sometimes be changed to a [ ` GET
` ](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/GET)

###  Parse Date Format

[ edit
](https://github.com/moment/momentjs.com/blob/master/docs/moment/10-plugins/14-parseformat.md)

    
    
    npm install moment-parseformat
    

This plugin extracts the format of a date/time string.

    
    
    var format = moment.parseFormat('Thursday, February 6th, 2014 9:20pm');
    // dddd, MMMM Do, YYYY h:mma
    moment().format(format); // format
    

That allows to create smart date inputs that let your users set a Date/Time
and lets you extract the user's preferred format for future usage. Find an
example usage of it at [ minutes.io ](https://minutes.io/new/Meeting) .

The Plugin has been authored by [ @gr2m ](https://github.com/gr2m) . Links: [ Demo ](http://gr2m.github.io/moment-parseformat/) | [ Source ](https://github.com/gr2m/moment.parseFormat)

#  torch.Tensor.storage_offset  ¶

](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int "\(in Python v3.12\)")
¶

    

Returns ` self  ` tensor’s offset in the underlying storage in terms of number
of storage elements (not bytes).

Example:

    
    
    >>> x = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
    >>> x.storage_offset()
    0
    >>> x[3:].storage_offset()
    3

](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_density_estimation) (KDE) is a non-
parametric way to estimate the probability density function (PDF) of a random
variable. This function uses Gaussian kernels and includes automatic bandwidth
determination.

Parameters  :

    

**bw_method** str, scalar or callable, optional

    

The method used to calculate the estimator bandwidth. This can be âscottâ,
âsilvermanâ, a scalar constant or a callable. If None (default),
âscottâ is used. See [ ` scipy.stats.gaussian_kde  `
](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.gaussian_kde.html#scipy.stats.gaussian_kde
"\(in SciPy v1.13.0\)") for more information.

**ind** NumPy array or int, optional

    

Evaluation points for the estimated PDF. If None (default), 1000 equally
spaced points are used. If  ind  is a NumPy array, the KDE is evaluated at the
points passed. If  ind  is an integer,  ind  number of equally spaced points
are used.

****kwargs**

    

Additional keyword arguments are documented in [ ` DataFrame.plot()  `
](pandas.DataFrame.plot.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot "pandas.DataFrame.plot") .

Returns  :

    

matplotlib.axes.Axes or numpy.ndarray of them

    

See also

[ ` scipy.stats.gaussian_kde  `
](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.gaussian_kde.html#scipy.stats.gaussian_kde
"\(in SciPy v1.13.0\)")

    

Representation of a kernel-density estimate using Gaussian kernels. This is
the function used internally to estimate the PDF.

Examples

Given a Series of points randomly sampled from an unknown distribution,
estimate its PDF using KDE with automatic bandwidth determination and plot the
results, evaluating them at 1000 equally spaced points (default):

    
    
    >>> s = pd.Series([1, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5])
    >>> ax = s.plot.kde()
    

![../../_images/pandas-Series-plot-kde-1.png](../../_images/pandas-Series-
plot-kde-1.png)

A scalar bandwidth can be specified. Using a small bandwidth value can lead to
over-fitting, while using a large bandwidth value may result in under-fitting:

    
    
    >>> ax = s.plot.kde(bw_method=0.3)
    

![../../_images/pandas-Series-plot-kde-2.png](../../_images/pandas-Series-
plot-kde-2.png)

    
    
    >>> ax = s.plot.kde(bw_method=3)
    

![../../_images/pandas-Series-plot-kde-3.png](../../_images/pandas-Series-
plot-kde-3.png)

Finally, the  ind  parameter determines the evaluation points for the plot of
the estimated PDF:

    
    
    >>> ax = s.plot.kde(ind=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
    

![../../_images/pandas-Series-plot-kde-4.png](../../_images/pandas-Series-
plot-kde-4.png)

For DataFrame, it works in the same way:

    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame({
    ...     'x': [1, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5],
    ...     'y': [4, 4, 4.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 6],
    ... })
    >>> ax = df.plot.kde()
    

![../../_images/pandas-Series-plot-kde-5.png](../../_images/pandas-Series-
plot-kde-5.png)

A scalar bandwidth can be specified. Using a small bandwidth value can lead to
over-fitting, while using a large bandwidth value may result in under-fitting:

    
    
    >>> ax = df.plot.kde(bw_method=0.3)
    

![../../_images/pandas-Series-plot-kde-6.png](../../_images/pandas-Series-
plot-kde-6.png)

    
    
    >>> ax = df.plot.kde(bw_method=3)
    

![../../_images/pandas-Series-plot-kde-7.png](../../_images/pandas-Series-
plot-kde-7.png)

Finally, the  ind  parameter determines the evaluation points for the plot of

    >>> ax = df.plot.kde(ind=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])

#  rank: Sample Ranks

##  Description

Returns the sample ranks of the values in a vector. Ties (i.e., equal values)
and missing values can be handled in several ways.

##  Usage

    
    
    rank(x, na.last = TRUE,
         ties.method = c("average", "first", "last", "random", "max", "min"))

##  Arguments

x

a numeric, complex, character or logical vector.

na.last

for controlling the treatment of ` [ NA ](/link/NA?package=base&version=3.6.2)
` s. If ` TRUE ` , missing values in the data are put last; if ` FALSE ` ,
they are put first; if ` NA ` , they are removed; if ` "keep" ` they are kept
with rank ` NA ` .

ties.method

a character string specifying how ties are treated, see ‘Details’; can be
abbreviated.

##  Value

A numeric vector of the same length as ` x ` with names copied from ` x `
(unless ` na.last = NA ` , when missing values are removed). The vector is of
integer type unless ` x ` is a long vector or ` ties.method = "average" ` when
it is of double type (whether or not there are any ties).

##  Details

If all components are different (and no ` NA ` s), the ranks are well defined,
with values in ` seq_along(x) ` . With some values equal (called ‘ties’), the
argument ` ties.method ` determines the result at the corresponding indices.
The ` "first" ` method results in a permutation with increasing values at each
index set of ties, and analogously ` "last" ` with decreasing values. The `
"random" ` method puts these in random order whereas the default, ` "average"
` , replaces them by their mean, and ` "max" ` and ` "min" ` replaces them by
their maximum and minimum respectively, the latter being the typical sports
ranking.

` NA ` values are never considered to be equal: for ` na.last = TRUE ` and `
na.last = FALSE ` they are given distinct ranks in the order in which they
occur in ` x ` .

**NB** : ` rank ` is not itself generic but ` [ xtfrm
](/link/xtfrm?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` is, and ` rank(xtfrm(x), ....) `
will have the desired result if there is a ` xtfrm ` method. Otherwise, ` rank
` will make use of ` == ` , ` > ` , ` is.na ` and extraction methods for
classed objects, possibly rather slowly.

##  References

Becker, R. A., Chambers, J. M. and Wilks, A. R. (1988) _The New S Language_ .
Wadsworth & Brooks/Cole.

##  See Also

` [ order ](/link/order?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` and ` [ sort
](/link/sort?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` ; ` [ xtfrm
](/link/xtfrm?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` , see above.

##  Examples

[ Run this code
](https://app.datacamp.com/workspace/preview?_tag=rdocs&rdocsPath=packages%2Fbase%2Fversions%2F3.6.2%2Ftopics%2Frank&utm_source=r-docs&utm_medium=docs&utm_term=rank&utm_content=run_example_in_workspace)

    
    
    # NOT RUN {
    (r1 <- rank(x1 <- c(3, 1, 4, 15, 92)))
    x2 <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5)
    names(x2) <- letters[1:11]
    (r2 <- rank(x2)) # ties are averaged
    
    ## rank() is "idempotent": rank(rank(x)) == rank(x) :
    stopifnot(rank(r1) == r1, rank(r2) == r2)
    
    ## ranks without averaging
    rank(x2, ties.method= "first")  # first occurrence wins
    rank(x2, ties.method= "last")   #  last occurrence wins
    rank(x2, ties.method= "random") # ties broken at random
    rank(x2, ties.method= "random") # and again
    
    ## keep ties ties, no average
    (rma <- rank(x2, ties.method= "max"))  # as used classically
    (rmi <- rank(x2, ties.method= "min"))  # as in Sports
    stopifnot(rma + rmi == round(r2 + r2))
    
    ## Comparing all tie.methods:
    tMeth <- eval(formals(rank)$ties.method)
    rx2 <- sapply(tMeth, function(M) rank(x2, ties.method=M))
    cbind(x2, rx2)
    ## ties.method's does not matter w/o ties:
    x <- sample(47)
    rx <- sapply(tMeth, function(MM) rank(x, ties.method=MM))

The function returns the encrypted value. The data type of the returned value
is VARIANT.
Although only a single value is returned, that value contains two or three
fields:
  * The first field is the initialization vector (IV). Both encryption and decryption use the IV. 
  * The second field is the ciphertext (encrypted value) of the ` _ value_to_encrypt  _ ` . 
  * If the encryption mode is AEAD-enabled, then the returned value also contains a third field, which is the AEAD tag. 
The IV and tag size depend on the encryption mode.
All 3 fields within the VARIANT are of type BINARY.

of boolean indicating whether each corresponding element is valid.

See also

[ ` isna  ` ](pandas.isna.html#pandas.isna "pandas.isna")

    

Boolean inverse of pandas.notna.

[ ` Series.notna  ` ](pandas.Series.notna.html#pandas.Series.notna
"pandas.Series.notna")

    

Detect valid values in a Series.

[ ` DataFrame.notna  ` ](pandas.DataFrame.notna.html#pandas.DataFrame.notna
"pandas.DataFrame.notna")

    

Detect valid values in a DataFrame.

[ ` Index.notna  ` ](pandas.Index.notna.html#pandas.Index.notna
"pandas.Index.notna")

    

Detect valid values in an Index.

Examples

Scalar arguments (including strings) result in a scalar boolean.

    
    
    >>> pd.notna('dog')
    True
    
    
    
    >>> pd.notna(pd.NA)
    False
    
    
    
    >>> pd.notna(np.nan)
    False
    

ndarrays result in an ndarray of booleans.

    
    
    >>> array = np.array([[1, np.nan, 3], [4, 5, np.nan]])
    >>> array
    array([[ 1., nan,  3.],
           [ 4.,  5., nan]])
    >>> pd.notna(array)
    array([[ True, False,  True],
           [ True,  True, False]])
    

For indexes, an ndarray of booleans is returned.

    
    
    >>> index = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2017-07-05", "2017-07-06", None,
    ...                          "2017-07-08"])
    >>> index
    DatetimeIndex(['2017-07-05', '2017-07-06', 'NaT', '2017-07-08'],
                  dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
    >>> pd.notna(index)
    array([ True,  True, False,  True])
    

For Series and DataFrame, the same type is returned, containing booleans.

    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame([['ant', 'bee', 'cat'], ['dog', None, 'fly']])
    >>> df
         0     1    2
    0  ant   bee  cat
    1  dog  None  fly
    >>> pd.notna(df)
          0      1     2
    0  True   True  True
    1  True  False  True
    
    
    
    >>> pd.notna(df[1])
    0     True
    1    False

# Configuring Your Home Router for Optimal Device Bandwidth: A Step-by-Step Guide

A well-tuned home network can make the difference between smooth, uninterrupted streaming and frustrating buffering, or between lag-free online gaming and choppy, delayed play. One of the most effective ways to manage your network traffic is by configuring your router’s **Quality of Service (QoS)** settings, along with complementary features like parental controls and basic firewall rules. This guide walks you through practical steps to prioritize bandwidth for specific devices, reduce latency, and maintain a secure and organized network.

---

## Understanding Quality of Service (QoS)

**QoS** is a feature found on most modern consumer routers that allows you to assign priority levels to specific devices or types of traffic. For example, you can ensure that your gaming console or streaming device gets more bandwidth than background downloads or less critical browsing.

QoS works by monitoring network packets and allocating available bandwidth according to the rules you set. This means that during heavy network usage—such as when multiple household members are streaming, gaming, and video conferencing simultaneously—your high-priority devices will still perform reliably.

---

## Step 1: Access Your Router’s Interface

1. **Find Your Router’s IP Address** – Commonly `192.168.0.1` or `192.168.1.1`. You can check your device’s network settings if unsure.
2. **Login** – Enter the username and password. If you haven’t changed these from the default, consult your router’s manual or look for a label on the device.

> *Tip:* Always change default login credentials to prevent unauthorized access.

---

## Step 2: Locate QoS Settings

The location of QoS settings varies by brand:

- **TP-Link**: Advanced → QoS.
- **Netgear**: Advanced Setup → QoS Setup.
- **ASUS**: Adaptive QoS in the main menu.

Once inside, you’ll typically see options to enable QoS and set rules based on device MAC addresses, IP addresses, or application types.

---

## Step 3: Prioritize Devices

Identify the devices that require the most reliable connection—streaming boxes, smart TVs, gaming consoles, or work laptops for video conferencing.

1. **Enable QoS**.
2. **Add Device Rules** – Select your device from the connected devices list.
3. **Set Priority Level** – Many routers offer categories like High, Medium, and Low. Assign *High* to latency-sensitive devices.

---

## Step 4: Optimize for Streaming and Gaming

For streaming services like Netflix, Hulu, or Disney+, prioritize the TV or streaming stick. For gaming, prioritize the console or PC and consider enabling **Game Traffic Optimization** if your router supports it.

Some routers allow you to prioritize traffic types (e.g., “Video Streaming” or “Gaming”) rather than specific devices. This can be useful if multiple devices are used for the same activity.

---

## Step 5: Configure Parental Controls

Parental controls are not just about restricting content—they can also help manage bandwidth. By setting time limits or blocking access for certain devices during peak hours, you free up bandwidth for priority devices.

In most routers:

- Navigate to **Parental Controls**.
- Add devices to the restricted list.
- Set schedules or filtering rules.

---

## Step 6: Apply Basic Firewall Rules

A firewall adds a layer of security and can indirectly improve performance by blocking unnecessary inbound or outbound connections.

1. Open **Firewall Settings**.
2. Block ports or protocols not required for your household’s activities.
3. Enable features like **SPI (Stateful Packet Inspection)** to monitor traffic more efficiently.

---

## Step 7: Test and Adjust

After applying QoS, parental controls, and firewall rules:

- Run speed tests on priority devices during peak usage.
- Play an online game or stream a video to gauge latency and buffering.
- Adjust priorities if you notice performance issues.

---

## Example: ASUS Router Adaptive QoS

On an ASUS router:

1. Go to **Adaptive QoS** in the dashboard.
2. Select **QoS Type** → *Gaming* or *Media Streaming*.
3. Drag and drop devices into the priority list.
4. Save settings and reboot the router.

A screenshot in this interface would show a simple drag-and-drop list, making device prioritization intuitive.

---

## Conclusion

By leveraging your router’s QoS settings, parental controls, and firewall rules, you can create a more efficient, secure, and enjoyable home network environment. Whether you’re streaming high-definition movies or competing in fast-paced online games, these configurations ensure your critical devices get the bandwidth they need—without being affected by less important traffic on your network. Regularly revisiting these settings will keep your network optimized as your household’s devices and usage patterns evolve.

##  3.3.  Special method names  Â¶

A class can implement certain operations that are invoked by special syntax
(such as arithmetic operations or subscripting and slicing) by defining
methods with special names. This is Pythonâs approach to _operator
overloading_ , allowing classes to define their own behavior with respect to
language operators. For instance, if a class defines a method named  `
__getitem__()  ` , and ` x  ` is an instance of this class, then ` x[i]  ` is
roughly equivalent to ` type(x).__getitem__(x,  i)  ` . Except where
mentioned, attempts to execute an operation raise an exception when no
appropriate method is defined (typically [ ` AttributeError  `
](../library/exceptions.html#AttributeError "AttributeError") or [ ` TypeError
` ](../library/exceptions.html#TypeError "TypeError") ).

Setting a special method to ` None  ` indicates that the corresponding
operation is not available. For example, if a class sets  ` __iter__()  ` to `
None  ` , the class is not iterable, so calling [ ` iter()  `
](../library/functions.html#iter "iter") on its instances will raise a [ `
TypeError  ` ](../library/exceptions.html#TypeError "TypeError") (without
falling back to  ` __getitem__()  ` ).  [  2  ]

When implementing a class that emulates any built-in type, it is important
that the emulation only be implemented to the degree that it makes sense for
the object being modelled. For example, some sequences may work well with
retrieval of individual elements, but extracting a slice may not make sense.
(One example of this is the ` NodeList  ` interface in the W3Câs Document
Object Model.)

# Efficiently Splitting Large Text Files in Python While Preserving Headers and Formatting

When working with large datasets stored in text files, one common challenge is managing file size for processing, sharing, or archiving. Splitting a large text file into smaller, more manageable files can improve performance, reduce memory usage, and facilitate parallel processing. However, a frequent requirement is that each split file must retain consistent formatting and any header or metadata rows from the original file. This ensures that the integrity of the data is maintained and that each segment can be used independently without additional preprocessing.

In this post, we explore Python-based approaches for achieving this goal, focusing on efficient file I/O operations, preservation of metadata, and continuity of related information across output files.

---

## Understanding the Requirements

Before diving into implementation, it is important to clarify what “consistent formatting” means in this context. For most structured text files—such as CSV, TSV, or fixed-width formats—this involves:

- **Preserving headers**: The first line (or lines) that define column names or metadata must be present in each split file.
- **Maintaining delimiters and encoding**: Output files should use the same delimiter (comma, tab, etc.) and character encoding as the original file.
- **Ensuring data continuity**: Related records, such as grouped data, should remain intact within the same split file if possible, avoiding fragmentation of logical units.

---

## Choosing the Right File I/O Strategy

Python offers several ways to read and write files. For large files, the preferred method is reading in chunks rather than loading the entire file into memory. This can be achieved using:

- **Iterative line reading**: Using a `for` loop directly on the file object allows processing line-by-line.
- **Buffered reading**: The `io` module provides buffering capabilities for faster I/O operations.
- **CSV module or Pandas**: For structured data, these libraries handle parsing and writing with minimal effort while preserving formatting.

When splitting files, it’s important to decide on the split size. This could be based on the number of lines, file size in bytes, or logical group boundaries.

---

## Implementation Outline

A typical workflow to split a large text file while preserving headers would involve:

1. **Open the source file** for reading.
2. **Read and store the header line(s)** separately.
3. **Initialize counters** to track lines written to the current output file.
4. **Iterate through the file line-by-line**, writing lines to the current split file until the desired limit is reached.
5. **When the limit is reached**, close the current file, open a new one, and write the header before continuing.
6. **Repeat until all lines are processed**.

This approach ensures that each output file begins with the same header and maintains the same formatting as the original.

---

## Preserving Metadata and Continuity

For files containing metadata beyond a simple header—such as timestamps, file source information, or grouped entries—additional care is needed. One strategy is to parse the metadata into a structure at the start and write it to each split file before the data rows. If the data is grouped, ensure that the splitting logic respects group boundaries, so that related rows are not separated. This may require buffering more than one group at a time or adjusting split sizes dynamically.

---

## Performance Considerations

Efficiency is key when working with very large files. To optimize performance:

- Use **context managers** (`with` statements) for file operations to ensure proper resource management.
- Minimize string operations inside the main loop; pre-compute repetitive values such as header strings.
- When using Pandas, consider the `chunksize` parameter in `read_csv()` to process data in blocks.
- Avoid unnecessary conversions between data formats during splitting.

---

## Testing and Validation

After splitting, it’s crucial to validate the output files:

- Verify that all files contain the correct header and formatting.
- Check that the total number of lines across all split files matches the original file.
- Ensure group continuity if applicable.
- Confirm that encoding and delimiters are consistent.

Automating these checks with Python scripts can save time and reduce errors, especially when splitting files regularly as part of a data pipeline.

---

## Conclusion

Splitting large text files in Python while preserving headers and formatting is a manageable task with the right strategy. By focusing on efficient file I/O, careful handling of metadata, and ensuring continuity of related data, you can create output files that are both smaller and independently usable. Whether working with CSVs, logs, or other structured text formats, a well-designed splitting process will maintain data integrity and streamline downstream operations.

Return group values at the given quantile, a la numpy.percentile.

Parameters  :

    

**q** float or array-like, default 0.5 (50% quantile)

    

Value(s) between 0 and 1 providing the quantile(s) to compute.

**interpolation** {âlinearâ, âlowerâ, âhigherâ, âmidpointâ,
ânearestâ}

    

Method to use when the desired quantile falls between two points.

**numeric_only** bool, default False

    

Include only  float  ,  int  or  boolean  data.

New in version 1.5.0.

Changed in version 2.0.0:  numeric_only now defaults to ` False  ` .

Returns  :

    

Series or DataFrame

    

Return type determined by caller of GroupBy object.

Similar method for Series.

Similar method for DataFrame.

](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.percentile.html#numpy.percentile

Examples

#  polars.Expr.top_k  #

Expr.  top_k  (

     _ k  :  [ int  ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int "\(in Python v3.12\)") |  IntoExprColumn  =  5  _ , 
     _ *  _ , 
     _ by  :  IntoExpr  |  Iterable  [  IntoExpr  ]  |  [ None  ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#None "\(in Python v3.12\)") =  None  _ , 
     _ descending  :  [ bool  ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool "\(in Python v3.12\)") |  Sequence  [  [ bool  ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool "\(in Python v3.12\)") ]  =  False  _ , 
     _ nulls_last  :  [ bool  ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool "\(in Python v3.12\)") =  False  _ , 
     _ maintain_order  :  [ bool  ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool "\(in Python v3.12\)") =  False  _ , 
     _ multithreaded  :  [ bool  ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool "\(in Python v3.12\)") =  True  _ , 
)  →  Self  [ [source]  ](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/main/py-
polars/polars/expr/expr.py#L2034-L2198) #

    

Return the ` k  ` largest elements.

This has time complexity:

\\[\begin{split}O(n + k \\\log{}n - \frac{k}{2})\end{split}\\]

Parameters  :

    

**k**

    

Number of elements to return.

**by**

    

Column(s) included in sort order. Accepts expression input. Strings are parsed
as column names. If not provided, each column will be treated induvidually.

**descending**

    

Return the k smallest. Top-k by multiple columns can be specified per column
by passing a sequence of booleans.

**nulls_last**

    

Place null values last.

**maintain_order**

    

Whether the order should be maintained if elements are equal.

**multithreaded**

    

Sort using multiple threads.

See also

[ ` bottom_k  ` ](polars.Expr.bottom_k.html#polars.Expr.bottom_k
"polars.Expr.bottom_k")

    

Examples

Get the 5 largest values in series.

    
    
    >>> df = pl.DataFrame(
    ...     {
    ...         "value": [1, 98, 2, 3, 99, 4],
    ...     }
    ... )
    >>> df.select(
    ...     [
    ...         pl.col("value").top_k().alias("top_k"),
    ...         pl.col("value").bottom_k().alias("bottom_k"),
    ...     ]
    ... )
    shape: (5, 2)
    ┌───────┬──────────┐
    │ top_k ┆ bottom_k │
    │ ---   ┆ ---      │
    │ i64   ┆ i64      │
    ╞═══════╪══════════╡
    │ 99    ┆ 1        │
    │ 98    ┆ 2        │
    │ 4
